Shelah
shē'lä
n. (third son of Judah by the daughter of Shua; the son withheld from Tamar, and head of the Shelanite family in Judah)
From Hebrew Shelah, connected with a root meaning to draw out or to be at rest. He is not to be confused with Salah son of Arphaxad, whose name the KJV spells differently.

Biblical Definition

Shelah is Judah's third son, born at Chezib (Gen 38:5), and his part in the narrative is entirely passive — he is the son who was promised and never given. Er and Onan, his elder brothers, were both slain by the LORD for wickedness, and by the custom later written into the law the widow Tamar had a right to the next brother. Judah made the promise and then hedged it: “Remain a widow at thy father's house, till Shelah my son be grown: for he said, Lest peradventure he die also, as his brethren did” (Gen 38:11). The parenthesis exposes him. Judah is not protecting Tamar; he is protecting Shelah from Tamar, whom he privately blames for two deaths that Scripture blames on his sons. Years pass. “She saw that Shelah was grown, and she was not given unto him to wife” (Gen 38:14) — and out of that broken promise comes Tamar's desperate stratagem, Judah's exposure, and the birth of Pharez, through whom David and the Lord Jesus descend. Shelah survives it all. He goes down into Egypt with the seventy (Gen 46:12), and the Shelanites are counted in the wilderness census as a family of Judah. The son who was withheld to protect the line was not the son the line ran through.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Shelah; in sacred history he is the third son of Judah, whom his father withheld from Tamar, and the head of the family of the Shelanites.

SHELAH, n. The third son of Judah by the daughter of Shua the Canaanite, born at Chezib.

He is to be distinguished from Salah, the son of Arphaxad, in the line of Shem.

Judah promised him to Tamar, the widow of his brethren Er and Onan, but did not give him.

He went down with Jacob into Egypt among the sons of Judah.

From him descended the family of the Shelanites, numbered among the tribe of Judah.

Key Scripture

Gen 38:5 — "And she yet again conceived, and bare a son; and called his name Shelah: and he was at Chezib, when she bare him."

Gen 38:11 — "Then said Judah to Tamar his daughter in law, Remain a widow at thy father's house, till Shelah my son be grown: for he said, Lest peradventure he die also, as his brethren did. And Tamar went and dwelt in her father's house."

Gen 38:14 — "And she put her widow's garments off from her, and covered her with a vail, and wrapped herself, and sat in an open place, which is by the way to Timnath; for she saw that Shelah was grown, and she was not given unto him to wife."

Gen 46:12 — "And the sons of Judah; Er, and Onan, and Shelah, and Pharez, and Zerah: but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. And the sons of Pharez were Hezron and Hamul."

Modern Corruption

Judah's withholding of Shelah is treated as prudent fatherhood rather than as the breach of duty Judah himself later confesses, and the levirate obligation is dismissed as primitive custom.

expand to see more

Read superficially, Judah looks careful: two sons dead, a third to protect. Scripture reads him otherwise, and so eventually does he. The deaths were judicial — Er “was wicked in the sight of the LORD; and the LORD slew him” (Gen 38:7) — and had nothing to do with Tamar. Judah left a widow in her father's house under a promise he had no intention of keeping, which in that world meant a life without protection, provision or children. When the truth came out he did not defend himself: “She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son” (Gen 38:26). The narrative asks the reader to see what Judah eventually saw — that a broken promise to a defenceless woman is not caution but injustice, and that God had noticed.

The levirate duty itself is commonly waved off as an artefact of a primitive society. But the law that Moses later codified (Deu 25:5-6) exists to protect exactly the person least able to protect herself, and to keep a dead man's name in Israel. It is the same instinct that produces the kinsman-redeemer, and it runs straight to Boaz, who performed for Ruth what Judah refused to Tamar — and to Christ, who is not ashamed to call us brethren and who redeems what we could not. A society is measured by what it does for the widow: “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Shelah (H7956), Shelah; yabam (H2992), to perform the duty of a husband's brother; 'almanah (H490), widow; Tamar (H8559), Tamar; tsadaq (H6663), to be righteous.

expand to see more

Hebrew Shelah (H7956) — Shelah; the third son of Judah, head of the Shelanites.

Hebrew yabam (H2992) — to marry a brother's widow, to perform the levirate duty.

Hebrew 'almanah (H490) — widow; the estate in which Tamar was left waiting.

Hebrew Tamar (H8559) — Tamar, palm tree; the widow Judah wronged and afterward vindicated.

Hebrew tsadaq (H6663) — to be just, righteous; Judah's verdict, “more righteous than I”.

Usage

"“Till Shelah my son be grown” — a promise made with no intention of keeping it."

"“She saw that Shelah was grown, and she was not given unto him to wife” — the years counted by the wronged."

"The son withheld to save the line was not the son the line came through."
